newsitem.title: CHINA: Hong Kong to stay world economic leader - new chief.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong to stay world economic leader - new chief.

text.p: Hong Kong must remain "the world's freest and most vibrant economy", new leader Tung Chee-hwa said on Tuesday, unveiling a bold policy agenda for China's latest and richest region.
Speaking on the first day under Beijing's rule, Tung declared: "Democracy is the hallmark of a new era for Hong Kong."

In a major policy address hours after Hong Kong rejoined China as a Special Administrative Region after 156 years of British rule, Tung tackled virtually every important economic issue confronting him.
Hours after Tung's government was sworn in, the Beijing-appointed legislature passed an omnibus bill activating laws which curb protests and funding of political parties.
Pro-democracy activists promptly vowed to stage more protests in Hong Kong and called on communist China to hold immediate legislative elections.
Democracy campaigners and Western leaders have been angered by disbandment of the popularly elected legislative council despite Tung's promise of elections by May next year.
The 60-year-old Shanghai-born shipping magnate, who replaced colonial governor Chris Patten, pledged: "We will preserve existing freedoms and lifestyle."

He issued a rallying call to the 6.4 million population to develop skills in this region, which lacks natural resources, and fend off challenges to Hong Kong's place as the world's seventh trading economy.
His inauguration speech as Hong Kong's chief executive targeted skyrocketing property prices, where speculation in the crowded territory has pushed values beyond the reach of ordinary homebuyers.
He committed his new government to bold measures to stamp out "rampant speculation" affecting Hong Kong's overall competitiveness.

Through sale of government-controlled land, Tung promised to release at least 85,000 flats a year for housing -- radically increasing the present flow of home units -- and aimed to achieve a home ownership rate of 70 percent within 10 years.
"We will devise a range of anti-speculation measures and monitor the market closely. We will take resolute action when it becomes necessary to do so," Tung said.
Tung also committed the government to developing a high technology sector -- an idea that has provoked serious objection from economists who argue forcefully against state intervention.

"We will promote the services sector and facilitate the development of value-added and high-technology industries," Tung said, arguing that this was the only way to keep Hong Kong "at the forefront of the new age.
"We must adopt positive measures to encourage investment in the information industry and infrastructure and nurture expertise in this area," Tung said.
He urged major reforms in education and language training to "combine the strengths of East and West", with ample resources, higher teaching standards and extended classes.

The new ascendancy of Mandarin, China's national language, is a challenge to Hong Kong's Cantonese speakers and business leaders are complaining that rival regional states have better standards of English, the international language of commerce.

But Tung's comments on education went beyond academic issues to reflect an Asian focus on family and social values. "We will encourage our young people to have all-round development covering ethics, the intellect, the physique, social skills and aesthetics," he said.

Tung also committed his government to proceed with a Mandatory Provident Fund, a compulsory pension plan proposed by the former British government, and to create a "Commission for the Elderly" to examine ways to help the old live well in a winner-take-all, free-market society.
